screens.body:
A requirement is a precise statement of what the system must do or how well it must do it. Functional requirements describe behavior: 'the app lets users reset their password.' Non-functional requirements describe qualities: 'password reset completes in under 30 seconds' or 'data is encrypted at rest.'

Vague wishes aren't requirements. 'Make it fast' is a wish; 'search returns in under 2 seconds for 10k records' is a requirement you can test.

check.question: Which of these is a testable requirement?

screens.heading: What counts as a requirement
screens.keyPoint: Requirements are precise and testable — wishes aren't.

screens.body:
Clients speak in mush: 'it should be user-friendly.' Your job is refining mush into testable statements. Ask 'what does that look like?' until you can write a sentence a tester could verify.

'User-friendly checkout' becomes 'a new user completes checkout in under 3 minutes without help, measured in usability testing.' Same wish, now measurable. Every vague adjective — fast, easy, secure — needs a number or a concrete scenario.

options: Ask what it looks like until it's measurable
Write it down word for word
check.question: When a client says 'make it fast,' you…

screens.heading: Refining mush into requirements
screens.keyPoint: Turn every vague adjective into something measurable.

screens.body:
You can't build everything first. MoSCoW sorts requirements into four buckets: Must have (the release fails without it), Should have (important but survivable), Could have (nice if time permits), Won't have this time (explicitly out of scope).

The magic is the W: writing down what you're NOT building prevents the most painful arguments later. Priorities are promises about order.
screens.heading: Prioritizing with MoSCoW
screens.keyPoint: Must / Should / Could / Won't — and write down the Won'ts.

screens.body:
A use case diagram shows who uses the system and what they can do. Stick figures are actors (users, admins, other systems). Ovals are use cases ('Place order', 'Refund payment'). A box around the ovals is the system boundary.

Lines connect actors to the use cases they participate in. One diagram gives a newcomer the whole system in thirty seconds — no code reading required.

options: Actors and the use cases they participate in
check.question: A use case diagram shows…

screens.heading: Use case diagrams
screens.keyPoint: Actors, ovals, and a system boundary — the system at a glance.

screens.body:
Behind each oval sits a written use case: a title, the primary actor, preconditions (what must be true first), then the main flow as numbered steps. Then the alternate flows: what happens when things go wrong — card declined, item out of stock.

The alternate flows are where the real design lives. Anyone can describe the happy path; professionals design the sad paths too.

options: Numbered steps for the main flow plus alternate flows
check.question: A good use case description includes…

screens.heading: Writing a use case
screens.keyPoint: Main flow plus the sad paths — that's the real design.

screens.body:
Scope creep is the slow addition of 'just one more thing' until the project collapses. The defense is change control: every new request gets written down, estimated, and approved — or explicitly deferred — before anyone codes it.

This isn't bureaucracy; it's honesty. 'Yes, and it costs two weeks — what should we drop?' beats silent overtime every time.

options: Write it down, estimate it, approve or defer it
Code it immediately to be nice
Ignore it and hope it goes away
check.question: When a new request arrives mid-project…

screens.heading: Taming scope creep
screens.keyPoint: Every change gets estimated before it's approved.

screens.body:
A requirement isn't real until the stakeholder who asked for it agrees you understood them. Validate with walkthroughs: read each requirement back to the client in plain language and ask 'is this what you meant?'

Get sign-off on the requirements model before design starts. Fixing a misunderstood requirement in a document costs minutes; fixing it in shipped code costs weeks.

options: The stakeholder agrees you understood them
You wrote it in a document
check.question: A requirement is validated when…

screens.heading: Validating with stakeholders
screens.keyPoint: Read it back, get agreement, then get sign-off.

screens.body: The Scrum Guide's product backlog section — scrum.org. The Agile Manifesto principles on changing requirements — agilemanifesto.org. (For the full formal standard, IEEE 29148 covers requirements engineering.)
